title: Concurrency Limiter
summary:
A concurrency limiter caps **how many requests are in flight at once**. Where a [rate limiter](#/sd/f/rate-limiter) asks "how many may start per second?", this asks "how many may be running right now?" It is usually a semaphore or a bulkhead with a limit `L`.

**Little's law** ties the two together: `in-flight = arrival rate x latency`. Latency is the dangerous variable. If a database slows from 150 ms to 1.5 s, the same 200 req/s now needs 300 slots instead of 30, even though the arrival rate never crossed any rate limit. Threads, connections and memory run out first. A concurrency limit fixes that by turning "slow" into "rejected fast" instead of "everything slow".

Working rules:
- **Size it from capacity:** `L ~ throughput you want x latency you expect`, bounded by the resource (DB connections, worker threads, GPU slots).
- **When full, reject quickly** (`503`), or wait in a *small, bounded* queue with a short timeout. An unbounded queue only converts overload into latency.
- **Always release in a `finally`**: a leaked permit permanently shrinks the limit.
- **One limit per dependency** (a bulkhead, see [compartments](#/sd/f/compartment) and [tenant isolation](#/sd/f/tenant-isolation)): a slow dependency can then consume only its own share of threads.
- **Adaptive limits** use AIMD or latency gradients: raise the limit slowly while latency is healthy, cut it multiplicatively on timeouts or latency growth, so the limiter finds the system's real capacity.

The limiter's rejections are what [load shedding](#/sd/f/load-shedding) and client [backoff](#/sd/f/backoff-jitter) have to cope with.

drills.q: A service handles 200 requests per second, each taking 150 ms on average. How many requests are in flight at steady state?
drills.explain: Little's law: 200 req/s x 0.15 s = 30 concurrent requests. A concurrency limit comfortably above this (e.g. 40) leaves headroom without letting a slowdown consume everything.

drills.q: The same service has a concurrency limit of 40 and rejects instantly when full. The database degrades and each request now takes 500 ms. Arrivals stay at 200 req/s. How many requests per second are rejected at steady state?
drills.explain: Max throughput = limit / latency = 40 / 0.5 s = 80 req/s. The other 200 - 80 = 120 req/s are rejected quickly. Without the limit, in-flight work would balloon to 200 x 0.5 = 100 and keep growing as latency rose.

drills.q: Traffic is a steady 100 req/s, comfortably under a 500 req/s rate limit. A downstream call slows from 50 ms to 5 s. With no concurrency limit, which statement best describes what happens?
options: Nothing, since the rate limit is not exceeded
In-flight requests grow from about 5 to about 500, exhausting threads, connections or memory, and healthy endpoints on the same service start failing too
The rate limiter automatically lowers the allowed rate to match latency
The load balancer retries and fixes the slowness
drills.explain: Arrival rate stayed the same, but in-flight = rate x latency rose 100x. Rate limits do not see latency; a concurrency limit does, because the slow calls hold their permits.

drills.q: The concurrency limit is reached. What is the best default behavior for a new request?
options: Queue it in an unbounded queue so no request is lost
Reject it immediately with 503, or let it wait briefly in a small bounded queue with a short timeout
Start it anyway, since a few extra requests are harmless
Block the caller's thread until a permit frees up, however long it takes
drills.explain: Queued requests still hold the client's timeout clock; with an unbounded queue most of them will be abandoned by the time they run. Failing fast keeps latency for admitted requests low and tells the caller to back off.

drills.q: A service has 200 worker threads shared by calls to `search` (fast) and `export` (calls a slow third party). The third party hangs and `export` calls occupy all 200 threads. How should limits be arranged?
options: One global limit of 200 across all calls
A per-dependency (bulkhead) limit, e.g. 20 for `export`, so it can never take threads needed by `search`
Add a rate limiter on `export` of 20 per second
drills.explain: The failure is shared-resource exhaustion; a bulkhead caps the blast radius. More threads postpone the same collapse, and a rate limit still allows unbounded in-flight work if calls hang.

drills.q: Put the life cycle of a request through a concurrency limiter in order.
items: The request arrives and tries to acquire a permit without blocking
A permit is granted (otherwise the request is rejected here with 503)
The call to the dependency runs under a timeout
The permit is released in a finally block, whether the call succeeded, failed or timed out
Latency and outcome feed the adaptive limit (grow slowly, cut on timeouts)
drills.explain: Releasing in finally is what keeps the limit accurate; releasing only on success leaks a permit per failure, and the limit shrinks to zero during an incident.
